title: Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas
subtitle: Explore projection, association, commissural and limbic fibre systems
altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical map of Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas with selectable regions and pathways.
learningObjectives: Identify the major components of the Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas.
Trace key inputs, outputs and connections in the Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas.
Interpret lesion patterns cautiously using distributed-network and clinical context.

sections.explainSimply: Explore projection, association, commissural and limbic fibre systems.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Location: Distributed myelinated fibre bundles connecting cortical, subcortical, brainstem and spinal regions across both hemispheres. Major subdivisions include corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, arcuate fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, fornix, optic radiations, corticospinal tract. Inputs include cortical neurons, thalamic nuclei, hippocampal formation, brainstem nuclei; outputs include contralateral cortex, ipsilateral cortical targets, subcortical nuclei, brainstem and spinal cord.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Disconnection may produce weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, neglect, visual-field deficits, amnesia or slowed processing depending on tract and network. Diffuse disease often causes broad inefficiency rather than a single focal syndrome.
sections.clinicalPearl: When grey matter looks intact but function is not, ask whether the pathway between nodes has failed.
sections.practicalExample: Select a region, trace its incoming and outgoing pathways, then compare healthy and lesion overlays before forming a clinical hypothesis.
sections.limitationsCautions: Named fasciculi overlap and tractography does not directly show axons or direction of information flow. Individual anatomy is variable and lesion-symptom mapping requires clinical correlation.

anatomy.position: Distributed myelinated fibre bundles connecting cortical, subcortical, brainstem and spinal regions across both hemispheres.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Interpreted relative to connected cortical, subcortical and vascular structures; boundaries and laterality must be checked in the selected view.
anatomy.bloodSupply: Supplied by multiple cortical and deep perforating arterial territories; watershed zones and small-vessel disease can selectively affect long tracts.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Disconnection may produce weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, neglect, visual-field deficits, amnesia or slowed processing depending on tract and network. Diffuse disease often causes broad inefficiency rather than a single focal syndrome.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.

quiz.question: Which fibre class connects the two cerebral hemispheres?
quiz.rationale: Commissural pathways, especially the corpus callosum, connect homologous and heterologous regions across hemispheres.

quiz.question: A small lesion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule may cause dense weakness because:
options: Many descending motor fibres are tightly packed there
quiz.rationale: Compact organisation means a small lesion can affect many corticospinal fibres.

quiz.question: What is a key limitation of diffusion tractography?
options: It infers fibre orientation from water diffusion and can misrepresent crossing fibres
quiz.rationale: Tractography is an indirect reconstruction and is vulnerable to crossing-fibre and modelling limitations.

pathwayTrace.title: Trace disconnection through major white matter
pathwayTrace.instruction: Choose a pathway, follow the connected fibre route, then switch to Disrupted to predict the functional consequence before reading it.

pathways.label: Interhemispheric transfer
pathways.summary: Commissural fibres coordinate homologous and complementary processing across hemispheres.
pathways.healthy: Callosal fibres permit rapid exchange of sensory, motor and higher-order information between the hemispheres.
pathways.disrupted: Callosal injury can produce disconnection phenomena whose expression depends on lesion location, extent and task demands; findings are not reducible to a simple left-versus-right split.

pathways.label: Descending motor projection
pathways.summary: Motor commands converge through projection fibres on the way toward brainstem and spinal targets.
pathways.healthy: Distributed cortical motor output converges through corona radiata and the compact internal capsule before descending in the corticospinal system.
pathways.disrupted: A small lesion where fibres are densely packed, especially the internal capsule, can produce disproportionately broad contralateral weakness compared with a similarly sized lesion in more dispersed white matter.

pathways.label: Dorsal language pathway
pathways.summary: Frontotemporal-parietal association fibres support phonological and speech-motor integration within a distributed language network.
pathways.healthy: Dorsal association fibres support rapid coordination among temporal, parietal and frontal language-related regions.
pathways.disrupted: Damage may contribute to impaired repetition, phonological processing or speech-motor integration, but the phenotype depends on tract segment, cortical involvement and individual language organisation.

pathways.label: Ventral semantic pathway
pathways.summary: Long ventral association fibres link frontal, temporal and occipital regions for multimodal integration.
pathways.healthy: Ventral pathways support integration of semantic, visual and affective information across distant cortical regions.
pathways.disrupted: Disconnection can alter semantic access or frontotemporal integration, but tract-function mappings are probabilistic and overlap with neighbouring networks.

lesionLab.title: White-matter localisation challenge
lesionLab.instruction: Use the symptom pattern to choose the tract or fibre system that best explains the disconnection. Then inspect the caveat.

cases.label: Case 1
cases.prompt: A sudden small deep lesion is followed by marked contralateral face-arm-leg weakness with relatively little cortical cognitive change.
cases.rationale: The internal capsule contains densely packed descending and ascending fibres, so a small lesion can affect a large proportion of motor output.
cases.caveat: This is a localisation exercise, not a diagnosis. Vascular mechanism, sensory findings, imaging and examination determine the actual lesion.

cases.label: Case 2
cases.prompt: Speech remains fluent and comprehension is relatively preserved, but repetition and phonological sequencing are disproportionately impaired after a dominant-hemisphere lesion.
cases.rationale: The arcuate fasciculus is a major dorsal language pathway linking temporal-parietal and frontal language systems, although contemporary models treat repetition as network-based rather than a single-tract function.
cases.caveat: Cortical injury and other dorsal-stream fibres may produce similar findings; individual language organisation varies.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare intact tracts with disconnection
clinicalComparison.instruction: Use tract anatomy to connect network communication with the cognitive pattern expected when transmission is disrupted.

comparisons.label: Corpus callosum

healthy.label: Interhemispheric transfer
healthy.summary: Homologous and specialised cortical regions exchange information across the commissural system.
healthy.mechanism: Callosal fibres support integration and transfer between hemispheres.
healthy.observable: Tasks requiring cross-hemisphere integration proceed without a callosal bottleneck.

pathology.label: Callosal disconnection
pathology.summary: Interhemispheric information transfer may be selectively impaired despite relatively intact cortical nodes.
pathology.mechanism: Commissural fibre injury limits transfer of sensory, motor or cognitive information between hemispheres.
pathology.observable: Disconnection phenomena can emerge depending on lesion location and task demands.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: A callosal lesion is a network communication problem; behavioural effects depend on which fibres and cortical systems are disconnected.
comparisons.assessment: Use tasks that require interhemispheric transfer and interpret with lesion extent and handedness/lateralisation.
comparisons.caveat: Complete textbook disconnection syndromes are uncommon; partial lesions, compensation and bilateral representations alter presentation.

comparisons.label: Dorsal language pathway

healthy.label: Frontotemporal language integration
healthy.summary: Dorsal association fibres support communication among posterior and frontal language-related regions.
healthy.mechanism: Long-range white matter coordinates phonological and speech-production processes across nodes.
healthy.observable: Repetition and phonological integration are adequate for the person’s baseline.

pathology.label: Dorsal language disconnection
pathology.summary: Injury can disturb communication across otherwise viable language regions.
pathology.mechanism: Reduced tract integrity interrupts timing and transfer across the dorsal language system.
pathology.observable: Repetition or phonological language difficulties may be prominent within a broader variable profile.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: The tract model explains why language disturbance can reflect disconnection rather than destruction of one named language centre.
comparisons.assessment: Examine repetition, phonology, naming and fluency alongside comprehension and lesion anatomy.
comparisons.caveat: Language pathways are distributed and variable; arcuate injury is not synonymous with one fixed aphasia syndrome.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked disconnection reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Test whether a suspected tract problem produces the functional disconnection pattern expected from that pathway.

cases.label: Callosal integration
cases.prompt: A patient shows unusual difficulty integrating information across the two hemispheres after a documented callosal lesion. What domain should be prioritised?
cases.rationale: A callosal hypothesis predicts difficulty transferring or integrating information across hemispheres rather than a global loss of knowledge.
observe: integration of lateralised visual or tactile information
discordance between intact unilateral skills and impaired transfer
supports: bimanual coordination difficulty disproportionate to unilateral motor skill
challenges: peripheral sensory or motor deficits explaining the asymmetry
cases.nextStep: Interpret alongside handedness, lesion extent and other white-matter involvement.
cases.caveat: Real callosal lesions often coexist with neighbouring tissue damage; classic disconnection syndromes are uncommon in pure form.

cases.label: Language disconnection
cases.prompt: Speech is fluent and comprehension is relatively preserved, but repetition is disproportionately poor. Which domain is the best first target?
cases.rationale: A dorsal language-pathway hypothesis is strengthened by a disproportionate repetition/phonological working-memory problem relative to comprehension and semantic access.
observe: repetition across word and sentence length
challenges: equivalent impairment across comprehension, naming and repetition
hearing impairment or severe dysarthria accounting for performance
cases.nextStep: Map the full language profile and imaging context rather than inferring an arcuate lesion from repetition alone.
cases.caveat: Language is network-based; dorsal stream disruption can involve multiple cortical and subcortical components beyond the arcuate fasciculus.
